setup.zh: 十月十三。你断着一根肋骨，怀里揣着舅舅的信：「你爹如今天天进黑松岭……膝盖比去年重了。」柴房里，饭桶，和三株外门弟子当杂草的回春藤。
setup.en: The thirteenth of the tenth month. A rib is broken, and in your coat is your uncle's letter: "Your father goes into the Heisong Ridge every day now… his knee is worse than last year." In the woodshed: Rice Bucket, and three stems of the vine the outer disciples call weeds.

recap.zh: 第一炉：三株回春藤，只出了一颗九道金纹的回春丹。吃了，一夜伤好；你把它装进辣椒油瓶，留给爹的膝盖。
recap.en: The first batch: three stems of vine, and only one spring-return pill with nine gold lines. Eaten, it would mend you overnight; you put it in a chilli-oil bottle, kept for your father's knee.

zh: 三株当杂草的回春藤，放进炉子，盖上盖。
「轰。」一团青紫色的火，一点都不烫。
en: Three stems of vine everyone calls weeds; in they go, lid on.
Whoomph. A blue-violet flame — not hot at all.

story.zh:
门外「笃笃笃」三声。他手忙脚乱，一把将小狰捞过来，往炉子上一放。小狰正睡得迷糊，四只爪子一抱，把炉子搂在肚皮底下，五条尾巴往上一盖，只露出一个红毛团子。小满把门拉得大开，自己往门框上一靠，身子把屋里挡了一半。

是周衡。他抱着账簿，看了看小满肿得只剩一条缝的左眼，看了看他捂着肋骨的那只手，道：「马师弟一早来过执事房。说你摔坏了，起不来，药园这几夜，他替你巡。」他顿了一顿，「我去园门口看了巡夜簿。昨夜那一格，有一个手印。」他没说那手印是什么颜色。小满道：「是我按的。今夜，我也巡。」周衡道：「你这个样子。」小满道：「巡得了。」周衡低头提笔，在账簿上写了一行，吹了吹墨：「月底盘账，只认账，不认脸。」说罢，抱着账簿走了。

小满想了很久，才想明白：昨天夜里的事，周衡知道；周衡也只认他那本账。

小狰从炉子上站起来，鼻子一抽一抽的，冲着后山的方向拱个不停。一只从小偷灵草长大的狰，隔着三里地，便闻得见哪片崖缝里长着一株没人要的草。药园里的灵草，一株一株都在周衡账上，顺一株出来，他这巡夜的便成了贼。他把饭桶揣进怀里，一瘸一拐，跟着小狰上了后山，一直到背阴的一面崖壁底下。石缝里长着一丛藤，叶子灰绿，细细的，卷着边，蔫头耷脑。他认得这东西，舅舅说过，济世堂收它，晒干了论斤卖给跌打摔伤的，一斤三文：回春藤。仙家眼里是杂草。石缝里统共三株，他连根带土挖了出来。

回到柴房，他把门闩上，这才想起来，他不会炼丹。他把《吐纳经》从怀里掏出来，正面看了三遍，没有；翻过来，背面那几行他原只当是虫蛀的印子，这一回看清楚了，是字，极小极细，像是有人拿一根头发蘸了墨描的。他分明记得，从前这背面只有三四行，如今一数，竟有七行：回春藤几株，根须留几分，火起之前如何以气温炉，火起之后如何以气引火，火候到了，炉自开，不可强开。这竹简自己会长字。

他照着那几行字，把三株回春藤一株一株剥开，根须掐掉三分，留七分，放进饭桶的肚子里，盖上盖子。然后盘膝坐好，两只手按在炉肚上，把肚子里那股暖，一点一点，引到手心，又从手心，引进炉子里。那股暖进了炉子，便像水进了沙子。他引到第七股，额头上已经见汗了，肚子底下那一团暖，薄了小半。他想起娘在灶间烙饼：火候没到，饼不起泡，你就得等；等不住，掀了锅盖，那饼便塌了。

「轰」的一声，炉子里腾起一团青紫色的火。那团火，不烫。它不往外蹿，只在炉子底下一圈一圈地转，青的，紫的，把整间柴房都照亮了。炉盖上那只小兽两只眼睛都睁开了，张着嘴，一口一口，像是在吃那团火，那模样，跟他爹喝上一口热酒的时候一模一样。

一炷香过后，炉盖自己弹了开来。一股香气冲了出来，香得小狰一头栽倒，四脚朝天。炉底躺着一颗丹，圆滚滚的，碧绿碧绿，透亮得像一滴凝住了的露水。丹身上有纹，他数了一遍，又数了一遍：九道，全是金的，一道挨着一道，像一个人一圈一圈地系着腰带。三株藤，一颗丹。

他知道一道纹是什么样子：舅舅说过，济世堂柜台上的琉璃罐子里也摆着回春丹，灰扑扑的，一道纹，几个黑点，一颗要五两银子。他手里这一颗，九道。
story.en:
*Tock tock tock* at the door. In a flurry he grabbed Little Zheng and plonked it on the furnace. Little Zheng, half asleep, hugged the furnace under its belly with all four paws and laid its five tails over the top, so only a red ball of fur showed. Xiaoman pulled the door wide open, leaned on the frame, and blocked half the room with his body.

It was Zhou Heng. Holding his ledger, he looked at Xiaoman's left eye swollen to a slit, at the hand holding his ribs. "Brother Ma came to the stewards' office first thing. Says you had a bad fall and can't get up, and he'll watch the herb garden for you these next few nights." He paused. "I went and looked at the watch book by the garden gate. Last night's box has a handprint in it." He didn't say what colour the handprint was. Xiaoman said, "I made it. Tonight I'll watch too." Zhou Heng said, "In this state." Xiaoman said, "I can watch." Zhou Heng lowered his head, wrote a line in the ledger and blew on the ink. "Month-end accounts: I go by the books, not by faces." And he went off with the ledger.

It took Xiaoman a long time to understand: Zhou Heng knew what had happened last night; and Zhou Heng went only by his books.

Little Zheng got up off the furnace, nose twitching, nuzzling and nuzzling toward the back mountain. A zheng raised on stolen herbs could smell, from three li off, which crack in the cliffs held a weed nobody wanted. The herbs in the garden were every one in Zhou Heng's ledger; take one out, and the watchman would be the thief. He tucked Rice Bucket into his coat and limped after Little Zheng up the back mountain, to the foot of a cliff on the shady side. In a crack grew a tangle of vine, grey-green, thin, curled at the edges, drooping. He knew it: his uncle said the Jishi Hall bought it, dried, by the jin, to sell for falls and sprains — three coppers a jin: spring-return vine. To immortals, a weed. There were three stems in the crack in all, and he dug them up, roots, earth and all.

Back in the woodshed he barred the door, and only then remembered that he did not know how to make pills. He took the *Scroll of Breath* from his coat; three times over the front, nothing; he turned it over, and the few lines on the back he'd taken for worm marks he now saw clearly were writing, tiny and fine, as if drawn with a hair dipped in ink. He was sure the back had held only three or four lines before; now he counted seven: how many stems of spring-return vine, how much root to keep, how to warm the furnace with qi before the fire, how to lead the fire with qi once it caught, and when the heat is right the furnace opens itself — do not force it. The scroll grew its own writing.

Following those lines, he peeled the three stems one by one, pinched off three parts of the roots and kept seven, put them in Rice Bucket's belly, and closed the lid. Then he sat cross-legged, pressed both hands on the furnace's belly, and drew the warmth in his own belly, bit by bit, into his palms, and from his palms into the furnace. The warmth went into the furnace like water into sand. By the seventh draw sweat stood on his brow and the warmth in his belly had thinned by a good part. He thought of his mother making flatbread at the stove: if the heat isn't right the bread won't blister, and you have to wait; can't wait, lift the lid, and the bread falls flat.

*Whoomph* — a blue-violet flame rose in the furnace. It wasn't hot. It didn't leap out; it only circled and circled in the bottom of the furnace, blue, violet, lighting up the whole woodshed. Both the little beast's eyes on the lid were open now, its mouth open, mouthful by mouthful, as if eating the flame — exactly the way his father looked over a mouthful of hot wine.

After one stick of incense the lid sprang open by itself. A fragrance burst out, so strong that Little Zheng keeled over, four paws in the air. On the floor of the furnace lay one pill, perfectly round, jade green, clear as a drop of frozen dew. There were lines on it; he counted them once, and again: nine, all gold, one next to another round the pill, like a man winding a sash round his waist turn by turn. Three stems of vine, one pill.

He knew what one line looked like: his uncle had said the Jishi Hall kept spring-return pills in a glass jar on the counter, dull grey, one line, a few black spots, five taels apiece. The one in his hand had nine.

exits.means: keeps the pill in a chilli-oil bottle for his father's knee, and keeps the night watch half a month on a broken rib

story.zh:
他把丹托在手心里，肋骨一抽一抽地疼。他知道这东西能做什么：吞下去，今夜断的骨头便接上了，肿便消了，今夜、明夜、往后的每一夜，他都能好好地站在药园里，月底稳稳地过账。马小宝那半句话，就落空了。

他把丹送到嘴边。

怀里那封信硌了他一下。**膝盖比去年重了，阴天下不了炕，晴天照去。**他爹拖着那条腿，一个人过断碑，往黑松岭里走，为的是两只兔子。

炉盖上那只小兽睁着眼睛，看着他。

他把手放了下来。

伙房的胖大娘有一只装辣椒油的小瓷瓶，空了要扔，他去伙房讨了来，在井边洗了七遍，还是一股辣味儿。他把那颗丹装了进去，塞紧，揣进怀里，贴着那封信。他在本子上只记了一行：**九纹回春丹一颗，在瓶里。给爹的膝盖。**

捎是捎不下去的。一个进门一个月、交不起公中的杂灵根，捎回家一颗济世堂一辈子没见过的丹，马三在门框上敲着短棍问：沈老大，你儿子在山上，偷了谁家的？他借了药房的笔，给舅舅回了一行：儿好，勿念。叫爹别进黑松岭。又摸出三文钱——他身上统共只有这三文——塞给那光脚的孩子。那孩子捏着三文钱，看了他半天，道：「你舅舅说了，三文钱他给过了。」把钱又塞了回来，挑起担子走了。

那天夜里，子时，他翻不过墙，照旧从豁口里爬出去，爬到药园，在巡夜簿上十三夜那一格，按了一个手印。

那以后的半个月，沈小满是断着一根肋骨巡的夜。

白天，他照旧去讲堂，照旧挑水，挑一担，歇三回，肩膀不敢换。饭堂里，马小宝天天端着空碗从他桌边经过，天天停一停，拿指头戳那一个地方：「师弟，好些了没有？」戳一下，他眼前白一下，嘴上道：「好些了，师兄。」

夜里，他坐在药园东角阿禾那一圈红线旁边，灵草中间。肋骨疼，一口气吸不到底，他就不吸到底，学那个萝卜筐里的孩子，肚子一鼓，一落，浅浅的，落得长长的。灵草夜里吐出来的那点气，稠得像娘过年熬的那一锅粥，一口一口落下去，肚子底下那一团暖，一夜往下坠一丝。小狰蹲在他脚边，冲着黑地里，一声不吭。

十五夜里，墙头上「沙」的一响，冒出一个脑袋来。小满没动。那人骑在墙头上，四下里张望，张望到他这里，停住了。

是老蔫。

月亮底下，两个人隔着半个园子，看了很久。一个坐在灵草中间，脸上还青着；一个骑在墙头上，手里攥着一只空布袋。老蔫的嘴动了动，什么也没说出来。他慢慢地，从墙头上退了回去，脚下一滑，墙外「咕咚」一声，接着是一瘸一拐、走远了的脚步。

天亮以后，小满在墙根草里捡到一张油纸，叠成方块，还带着一点甜香，纸角上印着一个红戳——县城那家点心铺子的戳。整个沉鼎观，吃得起这家桂花糕的，只有一个人。他把油纸夹进了巡夜簿里。巡夜簿上那一夜，他写：**墙头有人，回去了。没丢。紫玉参，四十一。**

到了十月廿五那一夜，他坐在灵草中间，一口气落下去，肚子底下「咚」的一声，那一团暖猛地往下一沉，沉得更深，像一块干了一冬的地，一镢头刨下去，又刨出一层来；刨开了，能盛的，一下子多了一倍。练气二层。

是他一夜一夜，断着一根肋骨，自己坐出来的。
story.en:
He held the pill in his palm, his ribs throbbing. He knew what it could do: swallow it, and tonight the broken bone would knit and the swelling go down; tonight, tomorrow night, every night after, he could stand properly in the herb garden and pass the month-end accounts without a wobble. Ma Xiaobao's half-sentence would come to nothing.

He lifted the pill to his mouth.

The letter in his coat dug into him. **His knee is worse than last year — on overcast days he can't get off the kang, and on clear days he goes anyway.** His father dragging that leg past the broken stele alone, into the Heisong Ridge, for the sake of two rabbits.

The little beast on the lid had its eyes open, watching him.

He lowered his hand.

The fat auntie in the kitchen had a little porcelain chilli-oil bottle, empty and about to be thrown out; he went to the kitchen and begged it, and washed it seven times at the well, and it still smelled of chilli. He put the pill in, stoppered it tight, and tucked it into his coat against the letter. In his book he wrote only one line: **One nine-line spring-return pill, in the bottle. For Dad's knee.**

Send it down he could not. A mixed root a month through the gate, who couldn't even pay the common fund, sending home a pill the Jishi Hall had never seen in its life — Ma San would rap his short club on the doorframe and ask: Shen the Elder, your son up the mountain — whose did he steal? He borrowed a brush at the dispensary and wrote his uncle one line back: Your son is well, don't worry. Tell Dad not to go into the Heisong Ridge. Then he took out three coppers — all he had on him — and pushed them at the barefoot boy. The boy held the coppers and looked at him a long time. "Your uncle said he's paid me the three coppers already." He pushed them back, shouldered his load, and left.

That night at midnight, unable to climb the wall, he crawled out through the drain gap as before, crawled to the herb garden, and pressed a handprint into the box for the thirteenth night in the watch book.

For the half-month after that, Shen Xiaoman kept the night watch with a broken rib.

By day he went to lectures as usual and carried water as usual — one load, three rests, never daring to change shoulders. In the refectory Ma Xiaobao passed his table every day with an empty bowl, stopped every day, and poked that one spot: "Brother, any better?" At each poke his sight went white, and his mouth said, "Better, senior brother."

By night he sat in the east corner of the garden beside Ah He's ring of red thread, among the herbs. His rib hurt and a breath wouldn't go all the way down, so he didn't take it all the way down; he did as the baby in the radish basket did, belly rising, falling, shallow, the fall long. The breath the herbs gave off at night was as thick as the pot his mother cooked at New Year, and breath after breath went down, and the warmth beneath his belly sank a hair each night. Little Zheng squatted at his feet facing the dark, without a sound.

On the night of the fifteenth there was a rustle on top of the wall, and a head came up. Xiaoman didn't move. The figure sat astride the wall, looking all round, and when its look came round to him it stopped.

It was Laonian.

Under the moon the two of them looked at each other across half the garden for a long time — one sitting among the herbs, his face still bruised; one astride the wall, an empty cloth bag in his fist. Laonian's lips moved; nothing came out. Slowly he backed down off the wall; his foot slipped, there was a *thud* outside, then limping footsteps going away.

After dawn Xiaoman found a sheet of oiled paper in the grass at the foot of the wall, folded square, still faintly sweet, with a red stamp on the corner — the stamp of that pastry shop in the county town. In all of Chending Temple only one person could afford that shop's osmanthus cake. He slipped the paper into the watch book. Against that night in the watch book he wrote: **Someone on the wall, went back. Nothing missing. Purple jade ginseng: forty-one.**

On the night of the twenty-fifth of the tenth month, sitting among the herbs, he let a breath fall, and beneath his belly something went *dong*; the warmth sank suddenly, deeper, like ground dried out all winter when a mattock bites in and turns up another layer; once turned, it could hold twice as much at a stroke. The second level of qi refining.

He had sat it out himself, night after night, with a broken rib.
